sections.section_title: Clinical Presentation and Early Course: From Semaglutide Exposure to Progressive Weakness
sections.description: This section introduces the patient’s baseline health, the temporal relationship to semaglutide exposure, and the evolution from an acute adverse reaction to a subacute neuromuscular syndrome. It frames why the case became concerning for more than simple drug intolerance or deconditioning.
subtopics: Baseline patient profile: age, comorbidities, functional independence, and pre-existing NAFLD
Indication for semaglutide use in obesity and fatty liver disease
Immediate post-dose reaction: nausea, vomiting, poor oral intake, dyspnoea, renal failure, and metabolic acidosis
Interpretation of the initial mild CK elevation and why it did not yet establish rhabdomyolysis
Clinical progression over 4 months: proximal muscle weakness, inability to sit or stand independently, dysphagia, and dysphonia
Red-flag features suggesting inflammatory or necrotising myopathy rather than deconditioning alone
Importance of medication timeline and exposure history in suspected drug-associated myopathy
Key historical negatives: no statin exposure, no relevant supplements, no family history of myopathy, no excessive exertion, and no substance use

sections.section_title: Essential Background: Immune-Mediated Necrotising Myopathy and Drug-Associated Muscle Injury
sections.description: This section provides the focused background needed to understand the case. It explains IMNM as a clinicopathologic entity, distinguishes it from toxic myopathy and rhabdomyolysis, and reviews why GLP-1 receptor agonists are biologically and clinically relevant in this context.
subtopics: Definition and core clinical phenotype of immune-mediated necrotising myopathy (IMNM)
Typical manifestations of IMNM: severe proximal weakness, dysphagia, marked CK elevation, and aggressive course
Histopathologic hallmarks of IMNM: necrotic and regenerating fibers, macrophage-predominant injury, and relative paucity of lymphocytes
Serologic associations: anti-HMGCR, anti-SRP, and the significance of seronegative IMNM
How statin-associated anti-HMGCR myopathy shaped current understanding of drug-triggered autoimmune myopathy
Distinguishing IMNM from direct toxic myopathy and from rhabdomyolysis based on timing, CK trajectory, persistence after drug withdrawal, and response to immunosuppression
GLP-1 receptor agonists: common uses, common adverse effects, and emerging concerns regarding skeletal muscle loss or muscle injury
Why a single-drug exposure may still plausibly act as an immune trigger
Clinical importance of recognizing atypical or novel medication associations in autoimmune myopathies

sections.section_title: Diagnostic Workup: Laboratory, Imaging, and Biopsy Evidence
sections.description: This section walks through the evaluation that established the diagnosis and excluded major mimics. It emphasizes how each test contributed to pattern recognition, severity assessment, and refinement of the differential diagnosis.
subtopics: Interpretation of CK elevation over time: initial modest rise versus later peak near 4000 U/L
Liver enzymes in myopathy: how AST and ALT can reflect muscle injury, and how concurrent fatty liver complicated interpretation
Inflammatory markers and basic screening tests: ESR, CRP, thyroid testing, complements, blood counts, and renal function
Autoantibody evaluation: broad rheumatologic serologies, myositis-specific antibodies, and the meaning of negative HMGCR and SRP testing
Clinical interpretation of isolated low-titer SS-B positivity with negative ANA and SS-A
MRI of the thighs: recognizing symmetric muscle edema as supportive evidence for inflammatory myopathy
Cardiac evaluation: troponin, BNP, echocardiography, and cardiac MRI in suspected extra-skeletal muscle involvement
Imaging to exclude associated systemic disease: high-resolution CT chest and abdominal imaging
Role of liver biopsy in separating chronic hepatosteatosis from muscle-derived transaminase elevation

Muscle biopsy findings diagnostic of IMNM: necrotic and regenerating fibers, acid phosphatase positivity, CD68-positive myophagocytosis, membrane attack complex deposition, and sparse CD3-positive cells
Why biopsy was pivotal in a seronegative case

sections.section_title: Differential Diagnosis and Causal Reasoning: Why Semaglutide-Associated IMNM Was Favored
sections.description: This section teaches the diagnostic reasoning process. It compares competing explanations for the patient’s illness and shows how the clinicians arrived at probable semaglutide-associated IMNM despite uncertainty and incomplete pre-exposure data.
subtopics: Constructing the differential for proximal weakness with CK elevation and bulbar symptoms
Rhabdomyolysis versus IMNM: contrasting expected clinical course, magnitude and timing of CK elevation, and treatment response
Drug-induced toxic myopathy versus autoimmune drug-triggered necrotising myopathy
Polymyositis, dermatomyositis, overlap myositis, inclusion body myositis, endocrine myopathy, and inherited myopathy as alternative considerations
Why lack of rash, interstitial lung disease, arthritis, sicca syndrome, and broad serologic negativity argued against connective tissue disease overlap syndromes
How longstanding biopsy-proven NAFLD explained persistent transaminitis better than occult pre-existing myopathy
Interpreting the cardiac abnormalities: possible myocarditis, stress cardiomyopathy, or nonspecific inflammatory involvement
Limits of inference: absence of a pre-semiglutide CK and inability to fully exclude smouldering pre-existing IMNM
Using temporal association, exclusion of alternatives, biopsy findings, withdrawal response, and short-course immunosuppression response to support probable causality
Application of WHO-Uppsala Monitoring Centre causality principles in adverse drug reaction assessment
Why rechallenge would be unethical in severe suspected immune-mediated toxicity

sections.section_title: Management, Outcome, and Clinical Lessons for Practice
sections.description: This section covers treatment decisions, monitoring, recovery, and the broader implications of the case. It highlights practical management principles for severe IMNM and the pharmacovigilance message raised by this report.
subtopics: Indications for urgent treatment in severe myopathy with dysphagia and major functional decline
Initial therapy: pulse intravenous methylprednisolone followed by high-dose oral prednisone
Rationale for adding IVIG in persistent weakness and severe disease features
Monitoring treatment response using strength, swallowing function, CK trend, and functional status
Balancing efficacy, infection risk, and comorbidity burden during immunosuppression
Management of complications during follow-up, including septic shock from urinary tract infection
Prednisone tapering strategy in a patient with rapid biochemical and clinical improvement
Why additional steroid-sparing agents or repeated IVIG were deferred
Outcome: normalization of CK, return to baseline function, discontinuation of immunosuppression, and resolution of cardiac abnormalities
Features suggesting a drug-triggered, self-limited autoimmune process rather than chronic idiopathic IMNM
Counseling on lifelong avoidance of semaglutide and likely class avoidance of GLP-1 receptor agonists pending further evidence
Pharmacovigilance implications: reporting rare adverse events as use of GLP-1 receptor agonists expands
Practical take-home points for clinicians evaluating post-medication weakness with CK elevation
